C4ISR ASSESSMENT PLAN

{PROMPT} What are the standards that SNC TRAX can translate?

SNC TRAX is essentially a **gateway/translator across tactical datalinks and mission-data formats**. Based on SNC’s published specs and older program reference docs, the standards/protocols it can translate / gateway include:

**MIL-STD tactical datalinks and gateway standards (SNC-listed)**

-   **Link-16 (J-series)** — **MIL-STD-6016F** ([Sncorp](https://www.sncorp.com/capabilities/snc-trax-software/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
-   **SADL (Situational Awareness Data Link)** — **MIL-STD-6016F** ([Sncorp](https://www.sncorp.com/capabilities/snc-trax-software/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
-   **JREAP (Joint Range Extension Applications Protocol)** — **MIL-STD-3011** (incl. JREAP A/C in product sheet) ([Sncorp](https://www.sncorp.com/capabilities/snc-trax-software/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
-   **VMF (Variable Message Format)** — **MIL-STD-6017 A–D** (incl. “D Cursor-on-target” in SNC spec listing) ([Sncorp](https://www.sncorp.com/capabilities/snc-trax-software/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
-   **Forwarding/Gateway** — **MIL-STD-6020** ([Sncorp](https://www.sncorp.com/capabilities/snc-trax-software/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Common mission-data formats referenced with TRAX**

-   **Cursor-on-Target (CoT)** — shown operationally as source data that TRAX moves/encodes into Link-16/SADL message types
-   **KLV (Key-Length-Value)** — listed in SNC TRAX specs ([Sncorp](https://www.sncorp.com/capabilities/snc-trax-software/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
-   **KML** — appears in TRAX ecosystem descriptions (not always shown on the base TRAX page, but referenced in TRAX Edge materials and internal architecture notes alongside KLV/CoT) ([Microsat Systems](https://www.microsatsystems.biz/capabilities/trax-edge/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Concrete “translation” examples called out in internal references**

-   **CoT → Link-16/SADL (J-series)**, including examples like **J2.0 IIU PPLI** and **J12.6 Target Sorting SPI**
-   TRAX described as enabling interoperability across **LINK-16 / SADL / MANET / SA Mode radios** (the last two are more “network/radio environments” than message standards, but they’re part of the interoperability
-   Related test reporting also describes an **Android TRAX/ATRAX app translating CoT into J-series for Link-16**, and a companion app translating CoT into K-series for e mapping an end-to-end “TAK/EUD → datalink” chain

If you tell me **which TRAX variant** you mean (classic TRAX vs TRAX Edge vs ATRAX-on-EUD) and **which direction** you care about (e.g., TAK/CoT → I can turn this into a clean “inputs ↔ outputs” matrix for your specific integration scenario.

{PROMPT} I am primarily interested in classic TRAX. Provide the data schema for each of its supported message formats as a JSON file and as an XML file.

Classic TRAX is built around **Cursor-on-Target (CoT)** (XML) and commonly handles **KLV** metadata and **KML** products, then **translates CoT-derived position/targeting into J-series messages for SADL and Link-16** (e.g., **J2.0 PPLI** and **J12.6 Target Sorting / SPI**).

CoT itself is an XML “W3” (what/when/where) message with required fields like event@version/type/uid/time/start/stale and point@lat/lon/hae/ce/le.  
For KLV↔CoT interoperability, MISB provides recommended conversions from **KLV metadata tags (e.g., ST 0601 / EG 0104)** into basic CoT message patterns (Platform Position and Sensor Point of Interest).

**Files you asked for (schema pack)**

These contain **one schema per classic-TRAX-supported format** (CoT, KLV subset used for KLV↔CoT conversions, KML subset) plus **abstract field models** for J-series outputs (J2.0 PPLI and J12.6 SPI). The J-series schemas are intentionally **not bit/word-level Link-16/SADL encodings**—they’re gateway-facing field models because the authoritative J-series encodings aren’t present in the internal sources we pulled for this answer.

-   [Download the JSON schema pack](sandbox://mnt/data/trax_classic_schema_pack.json)
-   [Download the XML (XSD) schema pack](sandbox://mnt/data/trax_classic_schema_pack.xsd)

{PROMPT} You know about my work with AresNet and about my role as an Army Reserve Cyber Warrant Officer. While OFFSET3 is waiting to be awarded its SBIR Phase I for AresNet, I have received a mission to perform active military duty as the deputy lead of the first ever assessment of the SOF Common Core Architecture (SCCA) during an upcoming exercise. I will be required to build assessment tools to measure the performance of the SCCA for processing kill chain data from sensor to COP to effectuator on unclassified and classified systems. I am building an ontology, first at the unclassified level, which I will be able to test on unclassified systems, before moving it to classified systems. From your scope note, I understand why you cannot include a complete definition of Link-16 and SADL bit encodings, but we can build an ontology that is entirely consistent with the MIL standards supported by TRAX, which will allow us to create tools that can be used everywhere. Post exercise, we will use Palantir Foundry tools, like Quiver to perform analysis of time series data associated with kill chains to determine where data is dropped, degraded, or distorted in uncontested, DDIL, and "max" DDIL

conditions. Correct structuring the objects in this ontology is of paramount importance. It should cover kill chain objects from sensor, transport, data fusion, COP/CIP, mission planning, transport, to effector.

**Executive Summary**

You can get to “usable everywhere” by separating **(1) semantic kill-chain objects** from **(2) message-format adapters** and **(3) assessment telemetry**—then enforcing that separation with schemas and validation guardrails (“ontology anchoring,” “YAML/schema interfaces,” and “schema validation guardrails”) . I’ve generated a **v0.1 unclassified ontology data model** as both **JSON Schema** and a **companion XSD**, designed explicitly for **sensor → transport → fusion → COP/CIP → mission planning → transport → effector** and for time-series analysis in Foundry/Quiver.

-   [Download JSON Schema](sandbox://mnt/data/scca_killchain_ontology_v0_1.schema.json)
-   [Download XSD](sandbox://mnt/data/scca_killchain_ontology_v0_1.xsd)

**Design Principle**

Your AresNet materials already point toward a layered, interaction-first ontology (“roles → tasks → apps → protocols”) and explicitly call out the need to model **effects across physical, EW, cognitive/decision, and C2/doctrine layers** . For SCCA assessment, the equivalent “layering” is:

1.  **Semantic layer (truth objects):** entities, observations, tracks, targets, tasks, engagements
2.  **Interop layer (adapters):** parsed fields from tactical standards (kept abstract—no bit-level encodings)
3.  **Assessment layer (telemetry):** checkpoints, degradations, metric samples (latency/jitter/loss/etc.)

This lines up with the “metrics collector + dashboard” concept you’ve already been evolving (per-node latency/jitter/packet loss, scenario controls, and end-to-end measurement) and the event-stream logging pattern (network events, data-stream activities, dashboarded metrics) .

**Canonical Kill-Chain Objects**

The v0.1 schema pack implements these as first-class records (append-only/time-series friendly):

-   **Entity**: Unit, Platform, Sensor, Gateway, FusionNode, C2Node, Effector
-   **Observation**: sensor-derived “phenomenon at time/location,” with quality + provenance
-   **Track**: system track state at time/location (supports J-series-like PPLI and track updates at an abstract level)
-   **Target**: target object (supports SPI-like “priority target location” at an abstract level)
-   **MessageEnvelope**: interop wrapper for “what standard did this come from, who sent it, and what parsed fields did we extract?” (abstract, not bit-level)
-   **KillChainInstance** + **StageCheckpoint**: explicit stage stamps for **Sense / Transport1 / Fuse / COP / Plan / Transport2 / Engage / Assess**
-   **MetricSample**: time-series metric points (e2e latency, drop rate, staleness, distortion rate, etc.)
-   **DegradationEvent**: explicit “dropped/degraded/distorted” events for DDIL and “max DDIL” analysis

Every object is designed to carry **time**, **provenance**, and **security label** as core fields—because that’s what makes cross-system, cross-network tracing defensible during post-exercise analytics.

**Interop Consistency With Classic TRAX Targets**

Within the schema, the **MessageEnvelope.standard** field is pre-enumerated to align with the classic TRAX translation targets we’ve been using in your unclassified modeling work:

-   **CoT**
-   **MISB KLV 0601 (subset)**
-   **KML (subset)**
-   **J-series (abstract) J2.0 PPLI**
-   **J-series (abstract) J12.6 SPI**

The intent is: *normalize everything into the canonical objects above*, while retaining a **parsed-payload snapshot** and **raw_ref pointer** for traceability, without embedding restricted bit-level specifics.

**Assessment Instrumentation Pattern**

To make Quiver analysis straightforward, treat the ontology output as two event streams:

1.  **Operational records** (Entity/Observation/Track/Target/Message)
2.  **Assessment records** (StageCheckpoint/MetricSample/DegradationEvent)

This matches the “metrics collector + dashboard” framing you already have (scenario control, network impairment knobs, node-level + E2E metrics) and the event logging approach (config changes, AI actions, network events, data stream activities) .

**Risks and Mitigations**

-   **Risk: ID collision across enclaves / gateways.**  
    Mitigation: enforce a canonical **entity_id (UUID)** + keep native IDs as attributes; use **correlation_id** in MessageEnvelope and KillChainInstance.
-   **Risk: “Telemetry drift” when different teams instrument differently.**  
    Mitigation: schema-driven checkpoints/metrics + automated validation guardrails (explicitly called out in the SBIR planning approach) .
-   **Risk: Mixing semantics with transport artifacts.**  
    Mitigation: keep transport details in MessageEnvelope/Transport events; keep truth in Entity/Observation/Track/Target.
-   **Risk: DDIL effects masquerade as “sensor truth changes.”**  
    Mitigation: represent loss/latency/jitter/corruption as **DegradationEvent** and **MetricSample**, not as edits to the semantic objects.

If you want, I can also generate a **mapping spec** (field-to-field “adapter contracts”) for each message type into this canonical model—built the same way you’ve been treating “schema interfaces” in AresNet.

{PROMPT} Please generate a mapping spec (field-to-field “adapter contracts”) for each message type into this canonical model—built the same way I’ve been treating “schema interfaces” in AresNet.

I generated **field-to-field adapter contracts** for **each TRAX “classic” message type** into your **SCCA kill chain canonical model (v0.1)**, using the same “schema interface” pattern you’ve been applying in AresNet: **declarative interfaces + strict validation guardrails + ontology anchoring** , plus **drift detection + version control** expectations at the interface boundary .

**Deliverables (download)**

-   [Adapter contracts as JSON](sandbox://mnt/data/scca_trax_classic_adapter_contracts_v0_1.json)
-   [Adapter contracts as XML](sandbox://mnt/data/scca_trax_classic_adapter_contracts_v0_1.xml)
-   (Extra) [Adapter contracts as YAML](sandbox://mnt/data/scca_trax_classic_adapter_contracts_v0_1.yaml)

**What’s inside (per message type)**

Each adapter contract includes:

-   **Source schema reference** (from your TRAX classic schema pack) + **on-invalid behavior**
-   **Target canonical schema reference** + **on-canonical-validation-failure behavior**
-   **Stage hint** (Sense / COP / Plan) to support downstream kill-chain stitching
-   **Outputs emitted** (one-to-many allowed), with explicit **field maps**, transforms, defaults, and quality rules
-   **Raw retention rules** (payload + raw_ref) so you can replay/forensics everywhere

Record emission patterns:

-   **CoT Event (minimal)** → Message + Entity (platform) + Track
-   **KLV ST0601 subset** → Message + Entity (sensor) + Track (sensor position) + Observation (frame center)
-   **KML subset** → Message + (Entity + Track) **per Placemark**
-   **J2.0 PPLI (abstract)** → Message + Entity + Track
-   **J12.6 SPI (abstract)** → Message + optional Entity (source) + Target

If you want, next step is a **kill-chain correlator contract** (how Message.correlation_id, Track.track_id, Target.target_id, and Foundry/Quiver timestamps roll up into KillChainInstance.stages[]) so you can measure “drop/degrade/distort” at each stage under uncontested/DDIL/max-DDIL.

{PROMPT} Produce a a kill-chain correlator contract (how Message.correlation_id, Track.track_id, Target.target_id, and Foundry/Quiver timestamps roll up into KillChainInstance.stages[]) so I can measure “drop/degrade/distort” at each stage under uncontested/DDIL/max-DDIL.

Here’s the **kill-chain correlator contract** you asked for—explicitly defining how **Message.correlation_id**, **Track.track_id**, **Target.target_id**, and **Foundry/Quiver timestamps** roll up into **KillChainInstance.stages[]**, with **drop/degrade/distort** detection for **uncontested / DDIL / max-DDIL** profiles.

**Download**

-   [Correlator contract (JSON)](sandbox://mnt/data/scca_killchain_correlator_contract_v0_1.json)
-   [Correlator contract (XML)](sandbox://mnt/data/scca_killchain_correlator_contract_v0_1.xml)
-   (Extra) [Correlator contract (YAML)](sandbox://mnt/data/scca_killchain_correlator_contract_v0_1.yaml)

**What it gives you (at a glance)**

-   **Correlation key priority**: correlation_id → track_id → target_id (with optional crosswalk + deterministic fallback hashing rule).
-   **Timestamp semantics**: event-time preferred, ingest-time fallback, watermarking for out-of-order.
-   **Stage mapping rules**: deterministic assignment into Sense / Transport1 / Fuse / COP / Plan / Transport2 / Engage / Assess, using canonical kinds and (optionally) Quiver-derived stage timestamps.
-   **Drop/Degrade/Distort logic**:
    -   **Drop**: missing stage within per-profile stage timeout; message gaps.
    -   **Degrade**: stage latency budget exceeded; quality decay; track staleness.
    -   **Distort**: spatial drift beyond bounds; unexpected ID flips; conflicting duplicates.
-   **Profiles** (threshold sets): uncontested, ddil, max_ddil, with stage timeout + latency budgets + drift thresholds + allowable ID changes.
-   **Outputs**:
    -   KillChain (assembled stages)
    -   Metric series (stage latency, e2e latency, drop/distortion rates, staleness)
    -   Degradation events linked to affected records when possible.

If you want the next increment, I can generate a **Foundry/Quiver “event taxonomy + metric naming contract”** that standardizes what each system must emit (broker receive, gateway forward, fusion publish, COP ingest, etc.) so the correlator can run with minimal per-system customization.

{PROMPT} Generate a Foundry/Quiver “event taxonomy + metric naming contract” that standardizes what each system must emit (broker receive, gateway forward, fusion publish, COP ingest, etc.) with detailed instructions on how to set it up in Quiver/Foundry.

Here’s the **Foundry/Quiver “event taxonomy + metric naming contract”** aligned to your existing **KillChain correlator contract** (i.e., it standardizes what each boundary system must emit so Quiver timestamps can roll up into KillChainInstance.stages[]).

**Downloads**

-   [JSON contract](sandbox://mnt/data/scca_foundry_quiver_event_taxonomy_metric_naming_contract_v0_1.json)
-   [XML contract](sandbox://mnt/data/scca_foundry_quiver_event_taxonomy_metric_naming_contract_v0_1.xml)
-   [YAML contract](sandbox://mnt/data/scca_foundry_quiver_event_taxonomy_metric_naming_contract_v0_1.yaml)

**What this contract standardizes**

**1) Checkpoint events (what every system must emit)**

A single **TelemetryEvent** schema covers boundary checkpoints like **broker receive, gateway forward, fusion publish, COP ingest**, etc., with a strict event-name taxonomy:

event_name = scca.\<stage\>.\<system_role\>.\<action\>

This contract defines the required stage set **Sense → Transport1 → Fuse → COP → Plan → Transport2 → Engage → Assess**, and provides a “must/should” emission matrix so you always have enough checkpoints to compute:

-   **Drop** = missing expected next checkpoint
-   **Degrade** = latency/jitter/throughput shifts under DDIL
-   **Distort** = payload hash mismatch / parse failures

It also carries the minimum ID keys you need for correlator assembly: correlation_id, track_id, target_id, message_id.

**2) Metric naming (how Quiver series stay queryable)**

It standardizes a small set of **metric families** (latency/loss/distortion/quality/network-degrade) and **unit-forward names** (e.g., \*_ms, \*_ratio, \*_bps) so you can build consistent dashboards across vendors and enclaves.

It also explicitly includes “classic” network-degrade metrics you’ve already been using in AresNet/EXata-style telemetry normalization—e.g., **throughput, pkt_loss, jitter, rtt, sinr**—as canonical metric tokens for reuse in SCCA scoring.

**3) SeriesId scheme (so you don’t blow up cardinality)**

Foundry time series syncs key on seriesId, so the contract includes a **seriesId template** that stays stable at operational scale (per run/profile/stage/system), while explicitly warning you *not* to create time series per correlation_id at high volume (keep those drilldowns tabular or as derived objects).

**How to set it up in Foundry/Quiver (implementation playbook)**

**Step 1 — Land the raw event log dataset**

Ingest system-emitted **TelemetryEvent** rows into Foundry as a dataset (batch or streaming). Require:

-   time_utc (occurrence time)
-   prov.ingest_time_utc (receiver ingestion time)
-   event_name, stage, system_entity_id

**Step 2 — Normalize + validate (Pipeline Builder or transforms)**

Create a normalized events table that flattens fields, enforces UTC timestamps, and validates required columns. (This becomes your truth table for audit + per-kill-chain drilldowns.)

**Step 3 — Build the time series points table (unpivot)**

Create a derived table shaped for time series sync ingestion:

-   seriesId (string)
-   timestamp (timestamp or long)
-   value (numeric or string)
-   optional ingestionTime

This is exactly the shape Foundry expects for time series syncs. ([palantir.com](https://www.palantir.com/docs/foundry/time-series/time-series-syncs/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Step 4 — Create a Time Series Sync**

Create a **time series sync** from the points table and map:

-   seriesId → Series ID
-   timestamp → Timestamp
-   value → Value
-   ingestionTime → optional

Foundry’s time series sync docs call these out as required columns and describe creation through Time Series Catalog or Pipeline Builder. ([palantir.com](https://www.palantir.com/docs/foundry/time-series/time-series-syncs/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Step 5 — Attach Time Series Properties in the Ontology**

Use the **time series setup assistant** to wire the sync into Ontology time series properties. ([Palantir Foundation](https://palantirfoundation.org/docs/foundry/time-series/time-series-properties?utm_source=chatgpt.com))  
If you’ll have many metrics per system, prefer the **linked “sensor object type” pattern** (a telemetry/sensor object linked to SystemEntity) rather than exploding properties directly on SystemEntity. ([palantir.com](https://www.palantir.com/docs/foundry/time-series/time-series-overview?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Step 6 — Build Quiver dashboards + investigations**

In Quiver, you can add time series primarily through Ontology time series properties (Add data → Time series). ([palantir.com](https://www.palantir.com/docs/foundry/quiver/timeseries-overview?utm_source=chatgpt.com))  
If you haven’t finished Ontology wiring yet, Quiver can also import time series **directly from a sync** for exploratory analysis. ([palantir.com](https://www.palantir.com/docs/foundry/quiver/timeseries-overview?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

For per-kill-chain debugging, Quiver can convert tabular event data to time series (useful for “waterfall” views), but note the tabular conversion limitations at scale and when multiple points share a timestamp. ([palantir.com](https://www.palantir.com/docs/foundry/quiver/cards-transform-table?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Step 7 — Derived series + alerting (optional but high leverage)**

Foundry supports **derived series** defined in the Ontology so your computed metrics (stage latency, drop ratio, distortion ratio) behave like first-class time series for Quiver/Workshop/Automate. ([palantir.com](https://www.palantir.com/docs/foundry/time-series/time-series-usage?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Key risks and mitigations (baked into the contract)**

-   **Clock skew masquerading as degrade** → enforce NTP/PTP discipline + always carry both time_utc and prov.ingest_time_utc (lets you sanity-check and fall back).
-   **Series cardinality explosion** → seriesId scheme avoids per-correlation-id time series; keep instance-level drilldowns tabular/derived objects.
-   **“Distort” blind spot** → require stable payload_hash on normalized payload (when policy allows) + parse status/error buckets.

{PROMPT} What data streams do I tell my teammates to record collect from each site and system (e.g. from TRAX, COMPASS, TAK, etc. What else?) during each phase of exercise execution (uncontested, DDIL, and "max" DDIL)?

Below is the **data-capture “shopping list”** I’d give teammates so you can prove (a) **drop**, (b) **degrade**, and (c) **distort** at **each kill-chain stage** across **uncontested → DDIL → max-DDIL**.

The guiding idea comes straight out of your prior TRAX/TAK measurement framing: **measure interruptions to time-stamped data**, then score **message/data loss, latency, handshake, discovery, and subscription** failures.

**1) Always-on streams (collect in every phase)**

**A. “Ground truth” time + run markers (everything depends on this)**

Capture these at **every site** and **every enclave**:

-   **Authoritative time source telemetry** (NTP/PTP status, offset, drift, step events) from each node.
-   **Exercise phase markers** as explicit events (start/stop, phase=uncontested\|ddil\|max_ddil, plus “scenario inject ID”).
-   **Clock-quality metadata** alongside every event stream (so latency can be separated from clock error).

Why: your entire methodology is “interruptions to collection of time-stamped data.”

**B. Canonical “observation events” (Quiver/Foundry)**

From **every system boundary** (broker receive, gateway forward, fusion publish, COP ingest, etc.), collect:

-   **Structured event telemetry** (the contract you’ve been building): one record per boundary crossing / processing decision.
-   **Error + retry events** (including queue/backpressure and drop counters).

This is how you directly score **loss + latency + handshake/discovery/subscription** symptoms.

**C. Raw message planes (so you can prove “distort,” not just “drop”)**

At minimum, collect **raw in/out** at:

-   **Ingress to gateway**, **egress from gateway**
-   **Ingress to fusion**, **egress from fusion**
-   **Ingress to COP/CIP**, **egress to clients/effectors**

Because TRAX/TAK ecosystems commonly bridge **CoT** and related tactical formats (and TRAX is explicitly tied to Link-16/SADL and CoT/KML/KLV patterns), you want raw captures at those translation seams.

**2) System-by-system capture list (what to pull from whom)**

**TRAX (and any TRAX-associated gateway)**

TRAX is positioned as an interoperability/routing bridge across tactical links and IP transports.  
Collect:

-   **TRAX application logs** (info + debug if feasible during test windows)
-   **Inbound/outbound message logs** (raw payload + parsed headers + translation result)
-   **Routing table snapshots + changes** (and any “joined/combined networks” config deltas)
-   **Health/heartbeat + internal queue depth + drop counters**
-   **Interface-level counters** (packets in/out, errors, retransmits where available)

**TAK ecosystem (ATAK/WinTAK/iTAK + TAK Server)**

Internal material explicitly frames TAK ingesting specific tactical message families (e.g., J2.0 PPLI, J12.6 target sorting), and a CoT translator/TAK integration path.  
Collect:

-   **TAK Server**: server logs, client connect/disconnect, subscription state, publish/ingest counters, store-and-forward/backlog metrics
-   **Clients (ATAK/WinTAK/etc.)**: client logs, plugin logs, CoT in/out (or export feed), UI event markers for key user actions (optional but powerful)
-   **Network captures** at TAK Server ingress/egress (pcap or NetFlow/Zeek—see Transport section)

**“COMPASS” (and any COP/CIP / mission app you’re assessing)**

I didn’t find a SharePoint source in the current connector set that defines COMPASS’ internal interfaces, so treat COMPASS as a **first-class boundary emitter**: it must produce the same **broker receive / processing / publish / error** telemetry as everything else.  
Collect:

-   **Ingress/egress message logs** (raw + normalized)
-   **Track store snapshots** (track updates, merges, drops, stale eviction events)
-   **Publish events** to downstream COP clients / effectors
-   **User/system actions** that cause state transitions (e.g., “track accepted,” “target nominated,” “mission generated,” etc.)

**Sensors and sensor gateways (where “truth” originates)**

A prior measurement pattern explicitly depends on **sensor data + metadata + timestamps** being captured end-to-end for post-mission measurement.  
Collect:

-   **Sensor product stream(s)** (detections/observations + confidence + geolocation + timestamp)
-   **If video/imagery exists**: at least metadata sidecar (KLV-like metadata if applicable), plus keyframes or clip references (full FMV is optional if bandwidth/storage is constrained)
-   **Gateway logs** (decode/encode, publish, retry, loss counters)
-   **Discovery/subscription transactions** (explicitly called out as an evaluation dimension)

**Transport layer (networks, radios, routers, SATCOM, MANET, TDL gateways)**

This is where DDIL/max-DDIL manifests as measurable impairment.  
Collect (by site and at key choke points):

-   **PCAP at boundary interfaces** *or* **NetFlow/IPFIX + Zeek-style logs** for scalable capture (or both). Capturing pcaps/logs + NetFlow/Zeek artifacts is already part of how OFFSET3 frames evaluator-grade telemetry pipelines.
-   **Link stats**: throughput, loss, jitter/latency probes, reconnection counts, routing changes
-   **Gateway device logs** (TDL gateway / MOJO-TRAX gateway style components appear in prior SOCOM evaluation diagrams)
-   **Handshake outcomes** (success/fail) at the session layer, because “ability/inability to establish network connection handshake” is an explicit MOP/MOE target

**Effector / fires / mission execution interfaces**

Even if the effector is simulated, you need the “last mile”:

-   **Mission tasking messages** (ingress/egress)
-   **Acknowledgements / weapon-release or simulated effect confirmations**
-   **Timing of execution vs. plan** (to measure end-to-end kill-chain latency and distortion)

**3) Phase-specific guidance (what changes by uncontested/DDIL/max-DDIL)**

**Uncontested (baseline fidelity)**

Use this phase to capture **maximum observability**, because it becomes your comparator.

-   Turn on **full structured telemetry** everywhere.
-   Prefer **pcap at every major boundary** (gateway, broker, fusion, COP server, TAK server).
-   Capture **subscription/discovery traces** so later failures can be compared.

**DDIL (controlled degradation)**

Keep **the same streams**, but add:

-   **DDIL “inject configuration” stream** (what impairments were applied, where, and when)
-   Extra focus on:
    -   **retry/backoff**
    -   **queue depth/backpressure**
    -   **store-and-forward behavior**
    -   **handshake/discovery/subscription failures**

**Max-DDIL (failure-edge behavior)**

Again, keep the same streams, but prioritize survivability evidence:

-   **Local, on-node logging** (assume intermittent export)
-   **State snapshots at boundaries** (routing tables, subscriptions, track-store state, backlog sizes)
-   **Drop proofs** (hard counters + raw “missing interval” evidence in time series)

This is where you’ll most clearly separate:

-   **Drop** = disappearance (no event + no payload)
-   **Degrade** = late/out-of-order/partial
-   **Distort** = wrong values / wrong association (needs raw payload + canonical record comparison)

**4) What else (beyond TRAX/COMPASS/TAK) should be on the collection plan?**

If your goal is “sensor → COP → effector” under impairment, the *other* must-have producers/collectors are:

-   **Message brokers / integration buses** (Kafka/RMQ/etc. if present): topic-level consume/produce offsets, lag, reject counts
-   **Fusion services** (multi-sensor correlation/track fusion): input set, merge/split events, publish cadence
-   **Cross-domain solutions / guards** (if any): allow/deny, transform, quarantine, latency
-   **Directory/identity services** (if auth impacts handshake)
-   **Platform health telemetry** (CPU/mem/disk, process restarts) to separate “network DDIL” from “node failure”

{PROMPT} How will we identify and isolate the data to save, in what format will we save it, and how will we get it from the edge to Foundy in the IL-6 cloud?

**Overview: “Evidence Packs” + 3-lane transport to IL-6 Foundry**

A clean way to keep SCCA assessment data usable (and court-defensible) is to treat **everything you save as an “Evidence Pack”** that is **keyed, partitioned, and immutable**, then moved to IL-6 Foundry using one of three transport lanes (streaming, store-and-forward, or offline). That gives you repeatable analysis for **uncontested / DDIL / max-DDIL** while preserving enough raw truth to debug “drop / degrade / distort.”

**1) Identify and isolate what to save**

**1.1 Collection keys (how you isolate)**

Every record and every file you save should be labelable by a small set of *always-present* keys:

-   **exercise_id** (e.g., SONIC_SPEAR_2026)
-   **run_id** (unique per iteration / vignette / lane test)
-   **ddil_profile** (UNCONTESTED \| DDIL \| MAX_DDIL)
-   **site_id** (range / node / stack location)
-   **system_id** (TRAX / COMPASS / TAK / MCS-COP / gateways / fusion / effectors)
-   **classification** (and handling caveats)
-   **timebase_id** (ties back to clock/offset evidence)

Treat these keys as both:

1.  **folder/partition keys** for storage, and
2.  **attributes (ABAC tags)** inside the structured data, so Foundry governance can enforce separation at query time (NextMRO calls out ABAC-based access controls and strong data-governance patterns for IL5/IL6 environments).

**1.2 Data products (what you isolate)**

Each Evidence Pack should contain **four categories**:

**A) Canonical, correlator-ready structured telemetry (your v0.1 contracts)**

-   normalized_events (from your event taxonomy contract)
-   time_series_points
-   foundry_quiver_timestamps (the correlator-ready timestamp stream)

**B) Raw source-of-truth captures (for replay and dispute resolution)**

-   Network: **PCAP/PCAPNG**, plus flow/IDS telemetry such as **NetFlow/IPFIX** and **Zeek logs** (FLOW explicitly cites NetFlow/Zeek and related telemetry as core captures).
-   If adapters drift or parsing fails, keep **portable “pcap/log bundles”** so you can deterministically replay and re-derive normalized events later.
-   Forward/edge collection may return through different channels depending on what is available (CCE describes PCAP sessions collected forward and “returned via different channels”).

**C) System observability and trace logs (to prove where loss happened)**

-   “Structured JSON logs carry correlation IDs” to trace an event end-to-end; build that into every system that emits your event taxonomy.
-   Include explicit failure capture (dead-letter queues/topics) so loss isn’t silent.

**D) Configuration + provenance snapshots**

-   Config snapshots of each node (versions, schema versions, routing tables, gateway rules, COP subscription settings)
-   Provenance artifacts: hashes, signing cert chain (where approved), and a manifest (below)

**1.3 Manifest (how you prove completeness)**

Every Evidence Pack should include a small machine-readable **manifest** that lists:

-   files included
-   byte sizes
-   SHA-256 hashes
-   start/end time coverage per file
-   producing system_id + software version
-   schema version for each structured dataset

This is the practical backbone for “prove we didn’t miss a stage” analysis.

**2) Save format (what format we store it in)**

**2.1 Structured telemetry (best for Foundry scale)**

Use **partitioned Parquet** for anything tabular/time-series at rest:

-   normalized_events → Parquet (partition by exercise_id/run_id/ddil_profile/site_id/system_id/date_hour)
-   time_series_points → Parquet (same partitioning, plus metric_name if helpful)
-   foundry_quiver_timestamps → Parquet *and* NDJSON (see below)

Why: Parquet is compact, columnar, and ideal for Foundry transform jobs and Quiver-style time-series analysis.

**2.2 Streaming / edge spooling (best for DDIL)**

Use **NDJSON (JSON Lines)** for “hot path” spooling on edge because it is:

-   append-friendly,
-   resilient under interruption,
-   easy to gzip,
-   easy to replay into Foundry later.

Keep the structured logs in **JSON with correlation IDs** (explicitly called out as trace-enabling).

**2.3 Raw captures**

-   **PCAPNG** (preferred) or PCAP, rotated by time/size
-   **NetFlow/IPFIX** in native export + decoded copies (optional)
-   **Zeek** in its native logs (gzipped)
-   System logs as NDJSON where possible

**3) Move it from edge to IL-6 Foundry (3 transport lanes)**

**Lane 1 — Uncontested: near-real-time streaming**

When comms allow, push telemetry continuously:

-   Edge emits events to a broker (Kafka/Event Hubs/etc.)
-   IL-6 ingest consumer writes to Foundry landing datasets (raw + curated)

Design for retries and duplicates: idempotent writes + backoff are explicitly highlighted as resilience techniques.

Also require failure visibility: route “poison” events to a dead-letter topic/queue rather than losing them.

**Lane 2 — DDIL: store-and-forward with deterministic replay**

When comms are intermittent:

-   Edge collector writes NDJSON “segments” + rotating PCAP/Zeek bundles into a **local spool**
-   A **forwarder** periodically syncs “sealed segments” to IL-6 when a path is available
-   Foundry ingests segments in order (duplicates safe via idempotency)

This matches the reality that edge return paths vary and may not be continuous.

**Lane 3 — Max-DDIL: offline export + later ingestion**

When there is effectively no network path:

-   Seal Evidence Packs on a schedule (e.g., every mission thread / every hour)
-   Export to approved encrypted media with manifest + hashes
-   Courier to a node with IL-6 access for bulk upload into Foundry

This is where the “portable pcap/log bundle” approach becomes mission critical.

**4) Time alignment (so Quiver correlation works)**

Correlation collapses if clocks drift. Require a **timebase evidence stream** at every site:

-   NTP/PTP status and offset logs from each host
-   periodic “heartbeat” events from each system stamped at source and at receipt
-   explicit cross-stream correlation strategy (timestamp synchronization and correlation mechanisms are called out as foundational).

**5) Practical “how we’ll do it” checklist for the team**

1.  **Deploy a Collection Sidecar** on each system (TRAX, COMPASS, TAK, MCS-COP, gateways, fusion, COP services, effectors) that writes:
    -   v0.1 contract events (NDJSON + gzip)
    -   system trace logs (NDJSON)
    -   config snapshots (on change + periodic)
2.  **Deploy a Site Sensor Kit** that captures:
    -   PCAPNG (rotate hourly)
    -   NetFlow/IPFIX and Zeek (if available)
3.  **Seal Evidence Packs** by run_id + ddil_profile + time window, produce manifest + hashes
4.  **Transport via lane 1/2/3** depending on comms
5.  **In IL-6 Foundry**, land in a raw zone first; only then produce curated datasets for Quiver/correlator transforms (this supports governance expectations for segregated data handling and cross-domain integration needs in higher-classification contexts).

**Key risks and mitigations**

**Clock drift masquerades as “drop/degrade.”** Mitigate with mandatory timebase evidence and periodic multi-system heartbeats.  
**Silent loss inside gateways/brokers.** Mitigate with correlation IDs in structured logs and dead-letter routing.  
**Parser/adapter drift under field conditions.** Mitigate with portable raw bundles (pcap/log) so you can re-derive truth later.  
**DDIL path unpredictability.** Mitigate with store-and-forward + sealing, because returns may occur “via different channels.”
